articles.summary: For many small-to-medium-sized businesses (SMBs), VMware has become too expensive. articles.title: There’s much more to the TCL P80 Ultra than standout screen tech
articles.summary: Credit: Paul Jones / Android Authority The most compelling phones don’t make you choose between strong everyday hardware and something genuinely different. Unique features can add plenty to the experience, but they don’t paper over the cracks if you’re not getting the specs your money deserves. TCL’s new P80 Series arrives this month with the specs to back up its headline features. The P80 Ultra leads the range with hardware that compares strongly with rivals in the same price range, making a strong case for the P80 Series as one of the best-value smartphone options in its segment. The P80 Pro and P80 carry many of those strengths further down the lineup, while the Ultra and Pro add industry-exclusive NXTPAPER technology as a clear competitive advantage.

Pixel phones always come with an extra heaping of criticism, warranted or not, but there are real concerns about this year’s Pro phones. They have less RAM than last year’s models, HiLight has already proven disappointing , the Tensor G6 chip isn’t a particularly big performance upgrade , and the phones are more expensive than ever before. Considering all that, it would be safe to assume the Pixel 11 Pro () and Pixel 11 Pro XL () aren’t good phones. However, after spending about three weeks with both of them, I don’t think that could be further from the truth.

articles.title: 4 reasons why I’ll always buy Samsung Galaxy phones over Pixels
articles.summary: Credit: Robert Triggs / Android Authority I switch phones for a living, so I don’t say this lightly: Google makes great phones. But “great” and “the phone I’d actually buy and recommend to friends” are two very different things. I’ve used Galaxy and Pixel phones for years, and I always come back to a Galaxy. And no, this has nothing to do with foldables, the S Pen, or any of that stuff that only matters to a small group of users. It’s because of the experience that actually counts when you’re living with the same device for two or three years. Samsung just gets more of that right, at least for me. The Pixel 11 lineup hasn’t changed that.

I’m a big fan of the simplicity of those early HDMI dongles, far more than I am of the overly verbose and often laggy Google TV . I suppose I’m still just attached to my earliest smart TV experience, flinging content at my TV from my phone rather than running the gauntlet of advertisements just to find my favorite show. If it ain’t broken, don’t fix it, as they say, and my Chromecast (3rd gen) still sees occasional use. In fact, I’ve been using it a lot more in the past couple of years to placate two impatient youngsters.

articles.summary: In May 2025, the Google Photos app got an incredible feature: the ability to manually create photo stacks . However, that automated process doesn’t always work as you’d like, leaving your Photos library more chaotic than you’d prefer. Manual stacking fixes that issue perfectly — but there’s been just one problem: it’s been exclusive to the Photos app on iOS . There’s been evidence of manual stacking coming to the Android app for a while, but month after month, it’s remained MIA.

articles.title: Building trust in agentic RAG starts with evidence
articles.summary: Basic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) follows a straightforward pattern. A user asks a question, the system finds relevant content in a knowledge base, and the model uses it to ground its answer. This works for simple lookups, but many real-world retrieval systems need more control over how and where they search. Agentic RAG lets an agent rewrite the question and choose where and how to search. It may query a knowledge base or an account system, combine lexical, semantic, and graph search, fuse the resulting scores, rerank candidates, discard weak results, and try again. This can find evidence that a single semantic search would miss. It also adds more decision points that should be supported by evidence, and a confident answer may not reveal the retrieval path that led to it.  &
